doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: 52nd Street and the Stuyvesant Casino dances
summary: The fading 52nd Street scene and the Stuyvesant Casino where swing veterans played for dancers as bebop took over.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well you must have been on your way to becoming pretty hip yourself, even maybe you didn’t even realize it.

I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were lucky and he was in town. And, you know, Billie Holiday at the Onyx Club. So there was still a lot going on. And this was, you know, still a vibrant time. There was downtown on weekends, there was the Stuyvesant Casino in the Central Plaza, where these guys, Bob Maltz and Jack Crystal, who is Billy Crystal’s father, they booked musicians that were available for relatively little. Because this was the time when bebop had come in and a lot of swing era musicians were not that well employed. You know guys with big names — you had Buck Clayton, you had Roy Eldridge, you had Hot Lips Page, you even had Coleman Hawkins once in a while, you had Sidney Bechet certainly, you had a whole bunch of people. And that was a buck and a quarter, and it was what they called a “beer racket” insofar as beer was about the only beverage that you could buy there, but you bought pitchers of beer, and there was dancing. And a lot of the customers were young kids from Brooklyn and the Bronx who liked to go dancing and also to go pick up girls; and you know, girls would come to pick up guys. There is a short film called “Jazz Dance” that was shot at the Central Plaza that gives you some of the flavor there. Willie “The Lion” Smith is in it and Jimmy McPartland. Bands were great.
